item.research_question: How does the addition of 5 at. % Zr to a CoCrFeMnNi Cantor High Entropy Alloy affect its melting temperature, microstructure evolution during recrystallization, and mechanical properties when processed via vacuum induction melting of pre-alloyed powders?
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders for 45 h at 400 rpm; vacuum induction melting at >1720 K for 30 min; cold rolling to 90% thickness reduction; annealing at 1143 K (Zr-modified) or 1043 K (base) for 30 min
item.test_conditions: XRD (35°–100° 2Θ); SEM-EDS; TEM (200 kV); micro-hardness (300 mN and 50 mN loads); mechanical spectroscopy (400–900 Hz, room temp to 700 K at 1.5 K/min)
key_findings: The Zr-modified alloy exhibits a lower melting temperature due to eutectic formation, with liquid phase formation at about 1470 K compared to 2500 K for traditional arc melting.
The recrystallization temperature of the Zr-modified alloy (1143 K) is higher than that of the base alloy (1043 K).

After recrystallization, the Zr-modified alloy shows an average grain size of (6.0 ± 1.5) μm in dendritic regions and (1.5 ± 0.5) μm in inter-dendritic regions, compared to (15 ± 2) μm for the base alloy.
The Zr-modified alloy contains a coherent second phase (inter-dendritic) with an FCC structure, which is Ni-enriched and Zr-concentrated.
Micro-hardness of the Zr-rich inter-dendritic phase is higher than the dendritic region in as-cast and cold-rolled states, but both phases converge to similar values after recrystallization.
The dynamic Young's modulus at 300 K is (130 ± 10) GPa for the Zr-modified alloy versus (140 ± 10) GPa for the base alloy.
No cracks were observed in the Zr-modified alloy after cold rolling, indicating no significant embrittlement despite Zr addition.
Both alloys maintain an FCC crystallographic structure after annealing, with lattice parameters of (0.358 ± 0.002) nm for the Zr-modified alloy and (0.359 ± 0.002) nm for the base alloy.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the strengthening and grain refinement to the precipitation of a coherent second phase and the influence of Zr solute atoms on recovery and recrystallization processes. Solute atoms impede dislocation climb and cross-slip, leading to finer grains. The coherent nature of the second phase boundaries minimizes impediment to dislocation glide, preserving ductility while enhancing strength through precipitation and lattice distortion.
item.limitations: The authors state that a more thorough investigation was not possible due to the limited amount of available material.
item.future_work: The authors propose that a more thorough investigation will be performed subsequently.
quotes: A measure of 5 at. % Zr was added, resulting in a liquid phase formation at about 1470 K [,,], to be compared with the 2500 K of a traditional arc melting process.

The fully re-crystallized micro-structure of this alloy, Figure 8d, presents finer equiaxed geminated grains with an average grain size of (6.0 ± 1.5) μm [] in the dendritic regions and of (1.5 ± 0.5) μm into the inter-dendritic regions
